plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the polar double integral of sin theta over the region R in the first quadrant outside the circle r = 2 and inside the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta). The figure shows both curves in polar coordinates: the circle r = 2 (blue) centered at the origin and the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta) (purple), which extends further to the right. The shaded region R (light blue) lies in the first quadrant between theta = 0 and theta = pi/2, bounded on the inside by the circle and on the outside by the cardioid; a red radial line at an intermediate angle shows a representative radial strip. The figure establishes the geometry of the integration region R needed to set up the polar iterated integral with inner limits from r = 2 to r = 2(1 + cos theta) and outer limits from theta = 0 to theta = pi/2.

interactions.label: Outer polar boundary
interactions.teaches: The formula for r as a function of θ determines the outer curve, where it meets the fixed circle r = 2, and therefore the size and shape of the polar integration region

interactions.label: θ
interactions.teaches: For each fixed angle θ in the first quadrant, the radial slice begins at the circle r = 2 and ends at the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos θ), giving the inner and outer limits of integration

demo_steps.title: Start at θ = 0
demo_steps.narration: Along the positive x-axis, the circle gives r = 2 while the cardioid reaches farther out to r = 4. The radial thickness of the region is largest here.

demo_steps.title: Sweep a radial slice
demo_steps.narration: As θ increases through the first quadrant, the red radial strip shows that every slice starts on the blue circle and ends on the purple cardioid.

demo_steps.title: Meet at θ = π/2
demo_steps.narration: At θ = π/2, the cardioid value equals the circle value, so the radial interval collapses to a point. This intersection gives the upper angular limit.

demo_steps.title: Change the cardioid
demo_steps.narration: Edit the outer boundary formula to see the purple curve, the shaded region, and the intersection angle update together. The integral limits come from the geometry created by the boundary equations.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: In polar coordinates, this region is naturally described by 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 and 2 ≤ r ≤ 2(1 + cos θ): θ selects a radial slice, and r fills the distance between the inner and outer curves.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean Cartesian-style polar diagram with black horizontal and vertical axes crossing at the origin. Draw the circle r = 2 in bright blue and the right-facing cardioid in purple, with the cardioid extending farther right than the circle and touching the circle at the top and bottom of the circle. Shade only the first-quadrant region between the circle and the cardioid in translucent light blue. Show a red radial line at the slider angle from the origin to the cardioid, with the portion between r = 2 and the cardioid reading as the representative strip. Place math labels near the same locations as the source figure: r = 2 on the left of the circle, r = 2(1 + cos θ) above the cardioid, θ = 0 near the positive horizontal axis, and θ = π/2 near the positive vertical axis.
